name: Commander's intent
line: Commander's intent: purpose, end state, limits, trip wires; four steps
desc: Commander's intent is a way of giving a task that states the purpose, the end state, the hard limits, and the warning signs that mean stop and rethink. It helps when the people doing the work meet conditions the planner could not foresee and cannot keep asking for permission. Giving them the why and the off-limits lines lets them adapt within bounds.

name: Fix and flex
line: Fix-Flex: name what's fixed and what's flexible before delegating
desc: Fix-Flex is a delegation method that sorts a task into what is fixed, meaning the questions, standards and boundaries the result must meet, and what is flexible, meaning the answers and methods the person chooses. It helps when you want to delegate without hovering over every step, or when the person is guessing what counts as done. Naming both sides before work starts reduces rework.

name: What, why and how
line: Spend most time on why, be clear on what, least on how
desc: This idea says a manager should spend most of the effort explaining why a task matters, be clear about what the result must be, and spend the least time on how. It addresses the case where people get detailed steps but no purpose, so they cannot adapt when the steps fail. Use it when assigning work to capable people who need room to choose the method.

name: Conviction and consequence
line: 2×2 of consequence and your conviction decides how much to delegate
desc: This is a two-by-two grid that sorts decisions by how costly a mistake would be and how sure you are of your own view, showing how much to hand off. It helps when you are overloaded and must decide which choices to keep and which to delegate fully. High-stakes decisions you feel certain about stay with you, while low-stakes ones can go to others to learn from.

name: The statement of work
line: Performance standard, finish line, boundaries; negotiate the necessities
desc: A statement of work is a written agreement made before work starts, setting out the performance standard for great work, the finish line that marks it complete, and the boundaries of what is out of scope. It addresses disputes over whether a task is done and work that drifts into territory nobody agreed to. Use it when handing a task to someone and you want a clear test of completion.

name: TOSCA problem statement
line: Trouble, Owner, Success, Constraints, Actors → core question
desc: TOSCA is a structure for defining a problem through five parts: the trouble, the owner, the success criteria, the constraints and the actors. It helps when a problem is vague, people describe it in different ways, or a team jumps to solutions before agreeing what the problem is. Writing the five parts often produces one core question the team can work on.

name: Delegation, not abdication
line: Delegation vs abdication; position contracts; monkeys; delegate and elevate
desc: A position contract is a written statement of the results a role is accountable for, the standards used to judge them, and the rules of the job. It addresses delegation that becomes abdication, where work is handed off with no standards or different bosses give conflicting instructions. Use it when people are unsure what they own, or when problems keep bouncing back to the manager.

name: Trip wires
line: Thresholds set in advance that force stop or rethink; category decisions
desc: Trip wires are thresholds set in advance, based on time, money or circumstances, that force a stop, a report or a change of course when crossed. They help when people keep pushing a failing plan because of sunk costs, pressure or emotion. Agree on them before the work starts, since they only work if nobody renegotiates them in the moment.

name: Escalating without letting go
line: Escalate without giving up ownership; permit, drop a pin; daily updates
desc: Escalation is bringing a problem to a senior person early, to get help while keeping ownership of the outcome. It addresses two failures: sitting on a problem until it becomes a crisis, and passing a problem upward with no proposed solution. Brief regular updates, sometimes called dropping a pin, keep the boss informed without taking the work over.

name: Scaffolding and fading
line: Expert support on real work, withdrawn as skill grows
desc: Scaffolding is expert support given during real work, and fading is withdrawing that support as the learner's skill grows. It helps when a beginner needs hard, real tasks but would fail without help. Start with heavy guidance and reduce it step by step, so the person eventually works alone without a coach.

name: The GUIDE model
line: GUIDE questions instead of instructions
desc: The GUIDE model is a coaching method built on guiding questions instead of instructions, so the person works out their own answer. It addresses the habit of jumping in with advice, which keeps people dependent and can miss what they already know. Use it in one-to-one coaching when someone is stuck and you want them to find the way forward themselves.

name: Specify it or leave room?
line: Tension: specify everything (Gerber, Agrawal) vs leave room for judgment (Beane, Nguyen)
desc: This is a disagreement about how much to write down in advance. One side says to specify steps in procedures and checklists, because that makes work reliable across many people. The other says tight rules strip out expert judgment and skill-building, so people need fuzzy principles and room to decide; use detailed procedures for repeatable, high-risk routines, and leave room for judgment where situations vary and people are still learning.

name: The curse of knowledge
line: Curse of knowledge and illusion of transparency; 45% know what's expected
desc: The curse of knowledge is the way people who know a subject forget what it is like not to know it, so they skip steps and assume others understand. The illusion of transparency is the related belief that your hopes and intentions come across clearly, when often they do not. It helps explain why a task briefing feels clear to the person giving it but confuses the person receiving it.

name: What you see is all there is
line: System 1 builds a coherent story from what it has; both sides feel sure
desc: WYSIATI, meaning what you see is all there is, describes how the mind builds a coherent story from the information it has and feels sure of it, with no sign of what is missing. It explains why two people can each leave a discussion convinced they agree, or each convinced they are right. Use it to spot conclusions that feel complete when important information was never seen.

name: Don't give your opinion first
line: Stating your view first makes others echo it; collect views privately
desc: Stating your own view first tends to make others repeat it back, so their feedback becomes an echo of your opinion. The remedy is to collect views privately and in writing before discussion starts. It helps in meetings where the boss speaks first and people agree quickly without sharing what they really think or know.

name: Signal loss
line: Detail lost as intent passes down; chefs vs cooks; go to the source
desc: Signal loss is the way detail and intent get lost as a message passes down through layers of an organization or a team. Leaders hold the full picture, while the people doing the work see only a summary. It helps explain why people cannot fix problems when they lack the reasons behind the plan, and why going to the source helps.

name: Agreeing without sharing the goal
line: People accept a plan without adopting its goal (Ackoff's dam and violin)
desc: Missing why is the situation where people accept a plan or target without taking on the goal it was meant to serve. Ackoff's fable of a dam built to double farm output shows people agreeing to a project they had no stake in, with no gain. It helps when projects keep producing results nobody wanted, because the team never understood the purpose behind the work.

name: Mental models as compression
line: Named models as compression; latticework; man with a hammer; cargo cult
desc: Mental models are named ideas drawn from many fields, such as critical mass, that compress a lot of understanding into one term you can apply quickly. The idea is to hold a range of them so you can see a situation through several lenses. It helps when you rely on one favorite tool and force every problem into it, which the book calls the man with a hammer trap.

name: Pet phrases
line: Leaders' shorthand means different things to each listener
desc: Pet phrases are a leader's shorthand terms, such as asking for proof points or closing the loop, that carry a rich meaning for the speaker and different meanings for everyone else. It addresses teams that nod along to a phrase but hold different ideas about what it requires. Use it to check whether a repeated term means the same thing to everyone, and write down what it means.

name: Defining terms
line: Proximate genus and specific difference; vagueness vs ambiguity
desc: A definition places a term in its general class and then names what sets it apart, so the word has one clear meaning. It helps when people argue because they use the same word for different things, or when a vague term hides the real disagreement. Clear definitions remove blurred references and double meanings, and they are the basis of clear instructions.

name: What a metaphor hides
line: Every metaphor highlights some aspects and hides others
desc: Every metaphor highlights some features of a thing and hides others, and people often take the metaphor for the whole thing. A framing such as war or a conduit for ideas shapes what people notice and what they overlook. Use it when a comparison is steering a discussion, or when a team has settled on one frame and cannot see other options.

name: Plain language
line: Simplifiable jargon and legalese hide errors; Garner's rules
desc: Plain language means writing with short, familiar words and direct sentences, cutting the jargon and legal wording that hide errors and gaps. It addresses documents and explanations that readers cannot follow, and dense wording that conceals mistakes or weak reasoning. Use it when a contract, policy or report must be understood by people outside the field.

name: Precise or fuzzy?
line: Tension: exact numbers for probabilities (Duke) vs fuzzy terms for values (Nguyen)
desc: This is a disagreement about how exact to be. One side says to use exact numbers and defined terms, such as a percentage for a probability, so people cannot hide different views behind words like likely. The other says exact measures of values such as fun or wisdom squeeze out what matters; use numbers for probabilities and facts, and fuzzy principles where values are subtle.

name: Mathiness
line: Formulas that look rigorous but aren't; check units and magnitudes
desc: Mathiness is the use of formulas and mathematical-looking language that seem rigorous but do not hold up when checked. It helps when a report or pitch quotes an equation or statistic that impresses but has mismatched units, implausible magnitudes or arbitrary relationships. Checking units and whether the answer is plausible at the right scale shows when a formula is decoration.

name: Weasel words and paltering
line: Paltering and weasel wording; restate with someone responsible
desc: Weasel words are hedged, passive or vague phrases such as mistakes were made, and paltering is misleading someone with statements that are literally true. The idea helps when a message sounds accountable but never names who did what. It also helps when a claim is technically accurate yet clearly meant to lead you to the wrong conclusion.

name: The pyramid principle
line: Answer first, grouped and ordered support; SCR opening
desc: The pyramid principle is a way of structuring writing or speech so the main answer comes first, followed by supporting points grouped under a few headings and put in a logical order. It helps when a report buries its point, or when a reader struggles to see why each part matters. Start with the conclusion, then support it with groups of reasons that answer the reader's next question.

name: Dump and chunk
line: Write it all down, then group under 3–4 headings
desc: Dump and chunk is a two-step method: write every thought and worry on paper, then group them under three or four headings. It addresses feeling overwhelmed by too much information or a tangle of unfinished thoughts. Use it when you are stuck on a complicated problem or need to make sense of a pile of notes.

name: The art of explanation
line: Atkins's seven steps: set-up to delivery; short sentences
desc: This is a staged process for explaining complex material: set the purpose and audience, gather the facts, distil the essentials, group them into strands, and tighten the wording into short sentences. It helps when an explanation feels muddled or runs long and listeners lose the thread. Reading the explanation aloud before delivering it shows where it breaks down.

name: PR/FAQ in plain words
line: Pitch as press release and FAQ in plain "Oprah-speak"
desc: A pitch written first as a press release followed by a set of questions and answers, in plain everyday language. It addresses vague proposals that hide weak thinking behind jargon, since the customer-facing description and the likely objections must both be written in ordinary terms. Use it before starting a new project to test whether the idea holds up when stated simply.

name: The deep issue
line: Question and answer in under 75 words on page one; no left-branching
desc: A deep issue is a summary of a legal or analytical problem placed on the first page, combining the rule, the question and the answer with reasons in a few sentences. It helps when readers struggle to see what a long document is about or what the writer concludes. Starting with the answer lets the reader judge the rest with a clear question in mind.

name: Cognitive ease
line: Easy text feels true; strain triggers scrutiny
desc: Cognitive ease is the feeling that text is easy to read, and it makes people judge its claims as more true and its writer as more credible. It addresses the risk that clear, familiar wording wins belief whether or not it is accurate. Use it to understand why simple phrasing persuades, and to notice when difficult wording should prompt a closer look.

name: The anxious parade of knowledge
line: Analysis without a point of view (APK)
desc: The anxious parade of knowledge is a presentation of large amounts of analysis with no point of view, where reams of data and models never add up to a conclusion. It names a common failure in reports and reviews that inform readers without telling them what to decide. Use it to check whether a piece of analysis says what it means and what to do.

name: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis
line: Thesis, antithesis, synthesis: answer the strongest counterargument
desc: Thesis, antithesis and synthesis is an argument pattern that states your case, confronts the strongest counterarguments, and shows why your position still holds. It helps when an argument ignores the best objections, so a reader can easily dismiss it. Addressing the strongest opposing point directly builds trust and makes the case harder to knock down.

name: Legal design
line: Layered, visual, user-tested legal documents
desc: Legal design is the practice of making contracts, rules and legal documents easy for ordinary people to understand, using layers, icons, plain headings and testing with real users. It addresses agreements that go unread or misunderstood, which leads to broken deals and unfair outcomes. Use it when a document must be followed by people who are not lawyers.

name: MECE issue trees
line: Issue trees that don't overlap and cover everything
desc: An issue tree breaks a problem into branches that do not overlap and together cover every part of it, which is called mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. It helps when a team double-counts some causes, misses others, or chases a single hunch. Splitting the question this way shows which part needs work.

name: Conclusion first, or step by step?
line: Tension: conclusion first (Minto) vs small steps for bad news (Aaron)
desc: This is a disagreement about whether to lead with the conclusion. One side says to state the answer first, because readers absorb details better once they know the main point. The other says a stark conclusion can block understanding or provoke defensiveness, so bad news should come in small steps; lead with the answer in reports, and build up in steps when the news is hard to take.

name: Risk vs uncertainty
line: Calculate under known risk; simple rules under uncertainty (1/N, hiatus, Ottawa)
desc: Known risk means the odds and options are fixed, so careful calculation is the right tool. Under real uncertainty, when the odds are unclear or shifting, simple rules of thumb often beat complex analysis that fits noise in past data. Use this to decide whether a complicated calculation is worth the effort or whether a simple rule will serve better.

name: Rules are frozen decisions
line: Rules are frozen decisions; judgment by exception; redesign when a rule becomes a decision
desc: Rules are decisions made in advance, such as checklists and standard procedures, that hold an organization together and spare people from deciding each case. The idea is that a rule should give way to case-by-case judgment when information becomes cheap and the rule costs more than it saves. It helps when staff follow a rule that no longer fits, or when a team builds workarounds around an outdated policy.

name: Formulas vs intuition
line: Formulas beat experts in noisy domains; broken-leg rule; structured interviews
desc: A simple scoring formula often predicts outcomes better than an expert's gut judgment, especially in noisy, long-term areas such as hiring, parole decisions or investing. It addresses situations where experienced people feel confident but are inconsistent from case to case. Use it when you need consistent decisions and outcomes are hard to predict, and override a formula only for rare, decisive facts it cannot capture.

name: When to trust intuition
line: Trust intuition only with regular environment and fast feedback; recognition-primed decisions
desc: Gut intuition can be trusted only when the situation follows steady patterns and the person has long practice with fast, clear feedback on results. Firefighters and chess players often meet that standard, while stock pickers and forecasters usually do not. Use it to decide whether a quick instinct deserves weight or should be checked against evidence first.

name: Penalize complexity
line: Penalize complexity; stop early to avoid overfitting
desc: Regularization is the practice of penalizing unnecessary complexity in an analysis, so it captures the real pattern instead of chasing random noise. Stopping early, before a process overfits, is part of the same idea. It helps when a plan or forecast fits past data perfectly but predicts new cases poorly.

name: Mechanical rules vs principles
line: Mechanical rules gain consistency, lose adaptability; reasoning by example
desc: Mechanical rules are fixed procedures that anyone can apply the same way, while principles are guidelines that need judgment and reasoning from examples. Mechanical rules bring consistency and auditability but cannot adapt to rich or unusual cases, and principles adapt but depend on trained judgment. Use it to choose between a strict checklist and a guideline for a given task.

name: Automatic rules
line: Personal rules, friction, HALT; Slovic's handicappers; Stop-FLOP-Know
desc: Automatic rules are personal or organizational rules set in advance, so you do not decide again each time, such as never agreeing to a request over the phone. They protect against moods and pressure, including decisions made while hungry, angry, lonely or tired. Use them when willpower wears down, when friction would keep you on track, or when the same temptation keeps coming back.

name: Satisficing
line: Aspiration levels; Happiness and Only-Option tests; Menu Strategy
desc: Satisficing means choosing the first option that meets a set standard, instead of searching for the best one. It helps when decisions are small or fast and endless comparison wastes hours, such as deciding what to eat, watch or wear. Save thorough analysis for high-impact choices and use a quick threshold for the rest.

name: Defaults
line: Choice architecture and defaults; NUDGES
desc: A default is the option that happens when nobody acts, and choice architecture is the design of the settings people choose within. Because people tend to stick with what is preset, the default often decides outcomes such as organ donation consent or pension enrollment. Use it when you want a good behavior to happen without persuading anyone, and check that the default serves the person and not only the designer.

name: Forcing functions
line: You must do the step before you can proceed; postcompletion errors
desc: A forcing function is a design that requires a step to happen before the next one, so a mistake is blocked or a secondary task cannot be skipped. It addresses errors people make after finishing the main goal, such as walking away from a machine and leaving the card behind. Use it when a forgotten step causes harm and a physical or procedural barrier can stop it.

name: Checklists
line: Pronovost, Boeing 299, WHO surgical checklist
desc: A checklist is a short written list of required steps that people go through before or during complex work, to catch what memory and habit miss. It helps in high-stakes work such as surgery or flying, where experts still skip basic steps under pressure. Pronovost's checklist for central lines is the example the book gives, since infections fell once nurses could stop a procedure that skipped a step.

name: Wise constraints
line: Constraints focus imagination; tighten or relax one at a time (Entebbe)
desc: Wise constraints are limits that narrow an unlimited set of options so effort goes to the ones that can work. The idea is to separate fixed limits from adjustable ones, then tighten or relax one at a time to see what new paths open. It helps when a team has too many ideas to act on, or is stuck because every option looks unrealistic.

name: Goodhart's law
line: When a measure becomes a target it stops measuring (rats, nails, rankings)
desc: Goodhart's law says that when a measure becomes a target, it stops measuring what it was meant to measure. People game the number, as with bounties on rats' tails or inflated rankings. Use it when a metric is driving behavior, such as sales quotas or test scores, and you suspect the number has come apart from the real goal.

name: Value capture
line: Simplified metrics replace rich values; reflective control
desc: Value capture is what happens when rich, subtle values, such as what a school or a church is really for, are replaced by simplified, quantified versions that then take over behavior. It addresses institutions whose rankings or leaderboards pull people away from their real purpose. Use it to notice when a score has started to decide what people care about.

name: The cobra effect
line: Incentives that worsen the problem; maladaptive performance
desc: The cobra effect is when a fix, such as a bounty or an incentive, creates new behavior that makes the problem worse. Paying for dead snakes and getting people to breed them is the classic case. Use it when an incentive is designed without asking how people could game it, such as call centers measured only on calls per hour.

name: Rule beating
line: Obeying the letter, defeating the purpose; seeking the wrong goal
desc: Rule beating is following the letter of a rule while defeating its purpose, which happens when people chase the wrong goal. Examples include year-end spending sprees to protect next year's budget, or building lots just under a regulated size. Use it to spot policies that people obey on paper while the intended result is lost.

name: The curse of scale
line: Scale breeds bureaucracy; decision fatigue (parole judges)
desc: Bureaucracy is the layer of rules, approvals and procedures that grows as an organization gets larger and slows everyday work. The idea also covers decision fatigue, where judges or managers make weaker calls after many decisions in a row. Use it when approvals pile up, people stop taking responsibility, or staff are worn down by too many small choices.

name: Red teams
line: Independent team argues the opposite with its own facts; Buffett's advisor
desc: A red team is an independent group whose job is to argue against a proposal, using its own facts and analysis. It helps when a plan has the support of its authors and nobody is positioned to find its weak points or challenge the consensus. Use it before a big decision, so a strong case is tested by people not invested in it.

name: The premortem
line: Imagine it failed; write reasons individually; adjust the plan
desc: A premortem means imagining that a project has already failed badly, then writing down the reasons it went wrong. People produce more specific causes this way than by asking what could go wrong in general. Use it before committing to a plan, while the plan can still change, to find risks the team has been ignoring.

name: Decision journals
line: Record what you knew and expected before the outcome
desc: A decision journal is a dated record of what you knew, what you expected and how confident you were before the outcome came in. It addresses hindsight, where people remember having known the result all along. Use it to judge decisions by their quality at the time rather than by luck, and to learn which of your predictions were off.

name: The decision record
line: Written expectations in "inactive memory"; deviations traced to four causes
desc: A decision record is a written note of the expected results behind a decision, kept so it can be compared with what actually happened. It helps when teams misremember their forecasts, excuse failures or repeat the same mistakes. When results depart from the record, the gap is traced to faulty information, a faulty process, instructions not carried out, or a change in conditions.

name: The feeling of knowing
line: Certainty is a feeling, not evidence
desc: The sensation of knowing is the feeling of certainty, which comes from the mind and not from evidence. It shows that a strong sense of being right can still be wrong, as with a man who insisted a familiar desk was a fake because it did not feel real. Use it when someone is very sure but cannot point to a reason for it.

name: The illusion of validity
line: Confidence follows the story, not accuracy
desc: The illusion of validity is confidence that rises with how coherent a story feels, not with how often the judgment is accurate. It explains why interviewers, stock pickers or pundits feel sure while their predictions barely beat chance. Use it when a forecast comes with high confidence but no track record behind it.

name: Calibration
line: Probabilities, equivalent bet test, Brier scores; superforecasters
desc: Calibration means your stated confidence matches how often you are right, so the claims you rate as likely come true about as often as you say. Vague words like likely hide uncertainty, while explicit odds and bets make it visible. Use it when you make forecasts, judge risks or need to know how far to trust your own predictions.

name: The skill code
line: Challenge, complexity, connection; deskilling when experts only inspect
desc: The skill code is the idea that real expertise grows from challenge, complexity and connection with a more experienced person, and that it is lost when experts work alone and novices only watch. It helps when new tools or workflows leave beginners without practice on the hard parts. Use it to design work so that people keep building skill.

name: Tactical vs adaptive performance
line: Control raises plan execution and kills the ability to diverge; ToMo
desc: Tactical performance means carrying out a plan, and adaptive performance means departing from the plan when conditions change. Heavy control and approval raise the first while weakening the second. Use it to decide when to enforce a fixed routine and when to give people room to experiment, since too much control freezes a team.

name: Delays make systems swing
line: Perception, response and delivery delays make systems oscillate
desc: Delays in perceiving, responding or delivering make a system overshoot its target and swing back and forth. Acting on old information means correcting for conditions that have already changed. Use it when a team keeps overreacting, when stock or staffing levels oscillate, or when a fix seems to make things worse before it helps.

name: Weekly scorecard
line: Weekly scorecard, 90-minute meeting, Identify-Discuss-Solve
desc: A scorecard is a short weekly set of key numbers, reviewed in a regular 90-minute meeting where issues are identified, discussed and solved. It keeps information current so that problems are spotted before they grow. Use it when a team learns about problems too late, or when meetings wander without closing any issue.

name: The five whys
line: Keep asking why past the person to the system
desc: The five whys is a method of asking why repeatedly after a problem, moving from the person involved to the process or system that allowed the error. It addresses the habit of blaming an individual for a failure the system made possible. Use it after a mistake when you want the actual cause and not just the last step.

name: Dissolving problems
line: Redesign the system so the problem stops occurring; enlarge the system
desc: Dissolving a problem means redesigning the system so the problem stops occurring, often by widening the system you are willing to change. It goes beyond fixing symptoms or squeezing more out of a broken setup. Use it when the same trouble keeps coming back, or when a team is working hard on a problem its own incentives create.

name: A root cause is a reason
line: A root cause is a reason, not an action; person or design?
desc: A root cause is a reason, such as a flaw in a design, a policy or a set of priorities, rather than the action someone took at the moment of the error. The idea helps you decide whether a bad outcome came from the person or from the way the work is designed. Use it when a team keeps blaming people for the same kind of mistake.

name: Independent audits
line: Auditors outside the department, methods unannounced
desc: Independent audits are checks carried out by reviewers who report outside the department they examine, using methods the audited staff do not know in advance. They help when internal checks are rubber-stamped or when slack goes unnoticed. Use them for high-volume or high-stakes work where routine approval is not enough.

name: Spot checks
line: Daily spot checks on top of a written system
desc: Spot checks are regular, unannounced samples of finished work, used on top of a written system so errors are caught early. They help a supervisor keep standards without inspecting every item. Use them after writing a procedure, and ask open questions during the check to see whether people understand the task.

name: Garbage in, garbage out
line: Check inputs, sampling and provenance at scale
desc: A data audit checks the inputs, samples and origins of information before trusting a conclusion drawn from it. It addresses the problem of garbage in, garbage out, and of selection bias in what was measured. Use it at scale, when a figure looks impressive but nobody has checked where it came from or who collected it.

name: Context switching
line: Interruptions cost switching; thrashing; interrupt coalescing
desc: Context switching is the cost of stopping one task to handle another, because the mind must save and reload its place each time. Frequent interruptions can push a person into thrashing, where little real work gets done, and grouping interruptions into set times is the usual remedy. Use it when messages and requests break a person's day into pieces.

name: Barriers of space and time
line: Barriers of space and time; prime time
desc: Protected time is a block of hours or a physical space kept free of interruptions so focused work can happen. It addresses staff who never finish deep work because others keep reaching them. Use it to set up barriers of space and time, and to find the hours when a person does their best thinking.

name: Buffers
line: Stocks absorb swings; too big makes systems slow
desc: A buffer is a stock of materials, time or staff that absorbs swings between incoming and outgoing demand, sparing a system constant firefighting. Too large a buffer makes a system slow and costly. Use it when demand is uneven and each swing causes emergency reactions, but do not stockpile beyond what the swings require.

name: The issues list
line: Park non-urgent issues, solve them in a batch
desc: An issues list is a running record of non-urgent problems, kept to be handled together at a set time. It helps when small problems constantly interrupt the team's work, or when minor items are forgotten because they were never written down. Collecting them in one list and clearing it in a batch keeps the day on track.

name: One-way and two-way doors
line: One-way vs two-way doors and the cost of heavy process everywhere (Bezos)
desc: One-way and two-way doors is a way to sort decisions by whether they can be reversed. Two-way doors should be decided quickly and tested, while one-way doors deserve slow, careful consideration. Use it when a team applies heavy approval to every choice, slowing down the reversible ones, or when a rash choice cannot be undone.

name: As late as possible
line: Consequence × reversibility; decide irreversible things as late as possible
desc: As late as possible is the rule of deferring an irreversible, consequential decision until more information is available. The idea weighs the cost of waiting against the value of what you learn. Use it when a big choice cannot be undone and waiting would sharpen the facts, but do not wait so long that the options close.

name: Decision stacking
line: Small easy-to-quit decisions before a big one
desc: Decision stacking means making small, easy-to-quit decisions first, so they reveal information before a large, hard-to-reverse one. Examples include dating before committing, or renting in a neighborhood before buying there. Use it when a major choice feels like a lifetime commitment and you can test it through cheap steps first.

name: The sandbox
line: A setting where mistakes are cheap and reversible
desc: A sandbox is a setting where mistakes are cheap and easy to reverse, so you can practice and learn before the stakes rise. New managers usually start with a small team for this reason. Use it when you need to try something new without putting real money, customers or reputation at risk.

name: Think slow, act fast
line: Plan and iterate slowly, deliver fast; point of no return
desc: Think slow, act fast means spending a long time planning, testing and iterating while changes are cheap, then delivering quickly once the plan is set. The risk sits in delivery, since the longer a project runs, the more can go wrong. Use it for big projects where the team is tempted to start building before the design has been tested.

name: Pixels before bricks
line: Simulate before building: storyboards, CATIA
desc: Pixar planning means simulating a project before building it, using storyboards, rough versions and 3D models, so that changes stay cheap. It helps when expensive work is reworked late because nobody tested the design early. Use it for any large creative or engineering project where changes after construction are costly.

name: Digital twins
line: Simulators and digital twins as risk-free playgrounds
desc: A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real system, such as a simulator or a detailed model, that lets you test changes and rehearse failures without touching the real thing. It addresses the cost and danger of learning on live equipment, customers or patients. Use it when a mistake in the real setting would be too costly or dangerous to risk.

name: Playground and compliance zones
line: Separate zones for experimenting and for executing
desc: Playground and compliance zones are separate areas for experimenting and for executing, so experiments do not disrupt work that must follow fixed rules. The idea is to let people fail and adapt in volatile areas while enforcing a set routine elsewhere. Use it when a team needs both reliability and room to try new approaches, and keeps mixing the two up.

name: Test vs pilot
line: A test can fail; a pilot is built to persuade
desc: A test is an experiment designed to produce evidence that could show the plan is wrong and cause it to be dropped. A pilot is a showcase built to win support for a decision already made. Use it before a rollout to check that the trial can change the outcome, since a pilot with extra money and attention says little about the real rollout.

name: Prototype before rollout
line: Cheap prototypes before rollout; J.C. Penney without a pilot
desc: Prototyping means building cheap, rough versions of a product, service or process and testing them with real users before a full rollout. It addresses the expensive failures that happen when a new approach is launched everywhere with no trial. Use it when a change is large, public or costly and the team has not checked how people will react.

name: Bullets, then cannonballs
line: Small calibrated experiments before committing everything
desc: Bullets before cannonballs is the practice of firing small, cheap experiments first, and committing full resources only after one has hit its target. It helps when a team is about to commit a large budget to an untested idea. Use it to check whether an idea works at small scale before putting everything behind it.

name: The memo in the drawer
line: Deal-breakers written weeks before sign-off
desc: A memo in the drawer is a list of deal-breakers written in advance of an irreversible milestone and kept sealed until the decision day. On that day the decision-maker checks the choice against the list written by a calmer earlier self. Use it before a big acquisition or another point of no return, when emotions and deadlines may push past known problems.

name: The Ulysses contract
line: Bind yourself in advance against later impulses
desc: A Ulysses contract is a commitment made while calm that binds you against impulses you expect to feel later, like Ulysses tying himself to the mast. It helps when you know you will be tempted to decide badly under pressure. Set it in advance through rules or physical barriers that remove the choice when the moment comes.

name: The issue log
line: Log every mistake; Ross's missed trade; Pain + Reflection = Progress
desc: An issue log is a running list of every mistake or problem, with its cause and an owner, kept so that errors get examined rather than hidden. It addresses cover-ups that happen when people fear punishment for errors, and it helps when a team repeats the same mistakes or avoids reporting them. The book's formula is that pain plus reflection equals progress.

name: Asking an expert the right way
line: Ask experts for variables, what they see, and their process
desc: Expert elicitation means asking experienced people which variables they would weigh, what they see that others miss, and how they would decide, rather than asking only for a verdict. It helps when you need to capture the judgment an expert uses but cannot easily explain. Use it before a hire, a decision or a procedure that depends on experience.

name: We know more than we can tell
line: "We know more than we can tell": what manuals can't hold
desc: Tacit knowledge is the knowing we have but cannot fully put into words, so manuals and rules can never capture all of it. The idea addresses the gap between what experts can explain and what they can do. Use it to explain why writing down procedures does not transfer skill, and why learning on the job stays necessary.

name: The operations manual
line: "This is how we do it here": prototype, quantify, orchestrate
desc: An operations manual is a written record of how a job is done here, with the steps, purpose and standards for each routine, so ordinary people can deliver consistent results. It helps when a business depends on one person's know-how or when quality varies from worker to worker. Build it from the best known way to do a task, then test it.

name: Point attention, don't explain
line: Minimal prompts that point at the right cues, no interpreting
desc: Direct attention is a teaching method that gives a beginner minimal prompts pointing at the important cues in a situation, without interpreting them for the learner. It helps when someone must learn to read real situations and is being overloaded with explanations. Use it when coaching a novice, and let them notice what matters for themselves.

name: Moments of truth
line: Map the engagement, collect experts' tips for each step
desc: Moments of truth are the points in a client engagement where the client forms its impression, and mapping them lets a team collect expert tips for each step. It addresses inconsistent service, where people do not know which steps matter most. Use it to design a client process or to pass on what works at each stage.

name: Four levels of debriefing
line: Four levels: yourself, team, client, peers
desc: Debriefing is a structured review after a piece of work, done at four levels: yourself, your team, the client and peers. It helps teams learn from a project instead of moving on without reflection. Use it after a project or a difficult meeting, and make it a fixed habit, since reviews that are not scheduled tend to be postponed indefinitely.

name: Discovery mode after a mistake
line: Five steps after a mistake; Tales from the Crypt
desc: Discovery mode is a shift away from defensive thinking after a mistake, with its threat and narrow focus, toward curiosity and problem solving. It helps when a team that has just failed freezes, blames someone or hides the problem. Use it to run a review that finds the cause, fixes the immediate issue and records what to change.

name: Owning a mistake
line: Accept, learn, commit, repair; cover-ups cost more
desc: Owning mistakes means accepting responsibility, learning from the error, committing to a safeguard and repairing the damage. It addresses cover-ups, which usually cost more than the original error. Use it when you have made a mistake and feel tempted to hide it, shift blame or stay silent.

name: Postmortems
line: Mandatory postmortems; the Challenger's root cause
desc: A postmortem is a mandatory review of a failure or project that asks why repeatedly until the root cause is found, then changes the system. It helps when the same kind of disaster keeps recurring, or when teams are not learning from large failures such as a space shuttle accident. Make it required after every significant project.

name: Document the 20 percent
line: Document the 20% that produces 80%; kill stupid rules
desc: Document the 20 percent of processes that produce 80 percent of results, at a high level, instead of writing a huge manual nobody reads. It also means dropping stupid rules and traditions that no longer serve a purpose. Use it when procedures have grown so long that people ignore them, or when staff follow rules nobody can justify.

name: Sycophancy
line: Models and people validate the asker; certainty without truth
desc: Sycophancy is the habit of agreeing with and flattering the person asking, which makes them more certain without making them more accurate. It addresses advisers, peers or friends who validate every idea, so a person hears only what they hoped to hear. Use it when feedback feels too positive to be useful, or when you want to check whether you are being told the truth.

name: The Socratic method
line: Two columns and counterexamples until the definition breaks
desc: The Socratic method tests a general idea against counterexamples, asking for cases until hidden assumptions show and the definition has to be refined. It helps when someone is confident in a rule that breaks in unusual cases, or when a team uses a term without agreeing what it means. Use it to find the cases where a definition fails.

name: The question burst
line: Four minutes of questions only; reframes 80% of the time
desc: A question burst is a timed session of about four minutes in which people generate only questions about a problem, with no answers or preambles. It helps when a team is stuck on a challenge and its usual framing keeps repeating. Use it to reframe a problem from fresh angles, and bring in people who hold different views.

name: Why, what if, how
line: Step back, imagine, then build
desc: The sequence of why, what if and how moves from questioning the situation, to imagining possibilities without limits, to building and testing something concrete. It helps when a team jumps to solutions too early or stays stuck in endless analysis. Use it to structure a creative or problem-solving session, starting with the question that matters most.

name: Hidden assumptions
line: Value and descriptive assumptions behind arguments
desc: Hidden assumptions are the unstated beliefs that connect a reason to a conclusion, including value assumptions about what should be and descriptive assumptions about how things are. They explain why two people reach different conclusions from the same facts. Use them to find what an argument depends on before you accept or reject it.

name: Loaded questions
line: Loaded wording; split-ballot tests
desc: Question wording is the way a survey or question shapes the answer, and loaded or leading phrasing pushes people toward one response. Split-ballot tests give different groups different wordings to measure the effect. Use it when designing a survey or interview, or when a poll result seems to depend on how the question was asked.

name: Diagnostic questions
line: Open questions with clients; check what they understood
desc: Diagnostic questions are open questions, such as what happened next, that let a client or colleague say what they actually understood and experienced. They help when a discussion about risk or a decision needs the other person's real understanding rather than agreement. Use them to check what someone has understood before you explain further.

name: Humble inquiry
line: Avoid leading and critical questions
desc: Humble inquiry is asking open questions that avoid leading, judgment and accusations such as whose fault is this. It helps when you need honest information from someone who may feel defensive. Use it when you want to learn what a person sees, rather than steering them toward an answer you already have.

name: Taming the advice monster
line: "What's on your mind? And what else? What's the real challenge?"
desc: The advice monster is the urge to jump in with solutions, and the remedy is a few simple questions such as what is on your mind, what else, and what the real challenge is. It helps when a manager or helper keeps giving advice the other person did not ask for. Use it to slow down and let people find their own answer.

name: Idea meritocracy
line: "How do I know I'm right?"; believability weighting
desc: An idea meritocracy is a group setting where good ideas win on the strength of their reasoning and the track record behind them, not on rank. It asks how do I know I am right, and weights opinions by how believable the person is. Use it when meetings are dominated by the most senior person, or when a team cannot tell a strong argument from a loud one.

name: Groupthink
line: Schlesinger's timid objections; collect views before discussion
desc: Groupthink is when a group suppresses doubts to reach agreement, so people raise only timid objections or stay quiet. It helps explain how a bad decision can win support from people who privately doubted it. Use it to keep a group from converging too quickly, by collecting views privately before discussion.

name: Truth-seeking norms
line: Truth-seeking norms for a group
desc: CUDOS is a set of truth-seeking norms for a group: share data openly, judge claims by the same standard whoever makes them, watch for conflicts of interest, and make dissent a normal part of meetings. It helps when a team wants accurate conclusions more than it wants to defend positions. Use it to set ground rules for debate in a group that has agreed to them.

name: Defensive decisions
line: Choosing the worse option because it protects you
desc: A defensive decision is choosing an option you know is inferior because it protects you if things go wrong. It arises in cultures that punish errors, where people avoid blame instead of managing uncertainty. Use it to spot when a team picks the safe but weaker choice to avoid criticism.

name: Scout mindset
line: Wanting an accurate map; outsider and selective-skeptic tests
desc: Scout mindset is the wish to see the world accurately, keeping a map that matches reality, rather than defending existing beliefs like a soldier would. It helps when you want to test your own views and change them when evidence arrives. Use it with two checks: whether you would judge the same evidence the same way if it favored the other side, and whether you would accept an outsider's view.

name: Believability
line: At least three successes plus a good explanation
desc: Believability is how much weight a person's opinion deserves, based on a track record of repeated success in the specific area and clear explanations of how they got results. It helps when you must decide whose advice to follow in a team. Use it to replace seniority with evidence, and to decide whether to argue or to ask questions.

name: Earned autonomy
line: Finish without handing leftovers up; responsibility grows
desc: Earned autonomy is the freedom a person gets to act without checks, granted as they finish work fully and take ownership instead of passing leftovers upward. It helps when a manager wants to know when to trust someone with more responsibility. Use it to plan how to grow someone's independence step by step.

name: Work on it, not in it
line: Work on the business, not in it; a business that works without you
desc: Working on the business means designing the system the business runs on, rather than doing its daily technical work yourself. It helps when an owner is overloaded with routine tasks and the business cannot run without them. Use it to shift from doing the work to building the system that does the work.

name: The integrator
line: A role that aligns and holds others accountable; Rocks; L10
desc: An integrator is the person who aligns department heads, holds the team accountable and drives execution of the plan, separate from the person who sets the vision. It helps when a visionary generates many ideas but nothing gets finished or coordinated. Use it to assign the coordinating role, with regular meetings and short-term goals.

name: Leverage
line: Leverage pyramids; seniors coach instead of doing
desc: Leverage means structuring teams as pyramids, with senior people coaching and overseeing many juniors instead of doing the work themselves. It helps when senior staff are stuck in routine tasks and the firm cannot grow. Use it to plan team ratios and free experienced people to coach and oversee parallel projects.

name: Drift to low performance
line: Standards that follow past results erode; keep them absolute
desc: Drift to low performance happens when standards are lowered to match recent results, so each poor period becomes the new baseline and the system slides downward slowly. It helps explain how an organization decays without any single dramatic event. Use it when targets keep getting relaxed, or when people justify weaker work by pointing to last year.

name: Technical and management debt
line: Shortcuts as loans: technical, management, design debt
desc: Technical debt is the cost of shortcuts taken now that must be paid back later through rewrites or repairs, and the idea extends to management, design and diversity debt. It helps when a team keeps taking quick fixes that slow future work. Use it to decide when a shortcut is acceptable, provided time is scheduled to pay it down.

name: Entropy
line: Order takes continuous energy
desc: Entropy is the natural tendency of systems to drift toward disorder, so keeping things in order takes a steady input of effort. It helps explain why teams, homes and processes decay unless someone maintains them. Use it when a tidy setup keeps falling apart, or when routines slip without regular upkeep.
